llm_text: You're not alone — there's no general law that says a product can only be sold for X% of its "actual value." There are anti-price-gouging laws that kick in during declared emergencies and antitrust laws to stop collusion, but otherwise businesses set prices based on costs, competition, and what customers will pay. If input costs (materials, labor, shipping, energy) go up, companies pass that along; if competition is weak or demand is inelastic, prices stay high. Prices also tend to be "sticky" — firms are slow to cut them when costs drop because of contract terms, menu costs, and the risk of losing margin. That's why fuel (a more spot-priced, fungible market) can fall quickly, while groceries, housing, and many manufactured goods lag.
